title: Does the Model Use the Feature?Separating Steering from Mechanism in LLMs

paper.title: Does the Model Use the Feature? Separating Steering from Mechanism in LLMs
paper.abstract: Abstract Internal features in LLMs are often interpreted as mechanisms when they track a concept and their manipulation changes a related behavior. Yet steering can push a feature far outside its natural range, where its effects need not reflect the model’s own computation. We examine this inference and propose an empirical contract whose tests evaluate features at values observed on natural inputs. One test copies a feature’s value from an input that shows a behavior into a matched input that does not (installation) or the reverse (removal); the other restores the feature after an upstream edit (downstream rescue). Installation measures how far the feature suffices for the behavior; removal and downstream rescue measure how much the model uses it. Applied to three kinds of representations, the two strengths separate sharply. The published unknown-entity latent strongly steers knowledge abstention, yet installing observed values from either published latent into matched prompts transfers only a small fraction of the natural known–unknown abstention contrast. Dense known–unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal in Gemma and Llama, and how fully a released subject–verb agreement feature set reproduces and restores the behavior depends on how its values are written into the model. Tracking a concept and steering a behavior therefore do not by themselves show that the model uses a feature, and each conclusion holds only for the intervention tested.

sections.heading: 1 Introduction
sections.text: Internal features offer candidate explanations for how LLMs produce behavior. Prior work links refusal to a single direction ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , organizes sparse features into interpretable causal graphs ( Marks et al., 2025 ) , and identifies sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents whose steering changes whether a model declines to answer questions about an entity ( Ferrando et al., 2025 ) , a behavior we call knowledge abstention . These results invite a mechanistic reading: if a feature tracks a concept and editing it changes the associated behavior, the model may use that feature to produce the behavior. But control is not the same as mechanism. Steering can drive a feature far beyond its natural range , the values it takes on natural inputs, and sufficiently large edits may recruit downstream pathways that the model does not ordinarily use. We therefore ask: when does feature-level control support a mechanistic interpretation of natural computation? We study this question with an empirical contract that distinguishes association, control, sufficiency, and use (Table 1 ). Association and control capture the familiar observations that a feature tracks a concept and that editing it changes behavior. The stronger claims ask whether the feature’s natural values reproduce the behavior ( sufficiency ) and whether the model’s own computation depends on the feature ( use ). We test both at values observed on natural inputs (Figure 1 ). In an interchange test ( Geiger et al., 2021 ) , paired inputs from two conditions exchange their feature values: installation transfers the value associated with the target behavior, while removal performs the reverse. In downstream rescue , we edit the model upstream, restore the feature downstream, and measure how much behavior returns. Our main audit focuses on the published entity-recognition latents of Ferrando et al. (2025) . We reproduce their separation of known and unknown entities and the strong steering effect of the unknown-entity latent. Yet setting the latent to a value within its natural range barely changes knowledge abstention; the behavior increases only when the latent is pushed beyond that range (Figure 2 ). Likewise, installing the known-entity latent’s common-name value into a prompt that names the same entity by a rare alias does not recover the accuracy gain of the common name. An independently fitted refusal direction serves as a positive control, showing that our tests detect effects at natural values when they are present. To separate a failure of the SAE basis from a failure of the underlying concept, we also test dense known–unknown directions defined by class-mean differences. Their behavior is asymmetric across models: Llama shows strong installation but weak removal and rescue, whereas Gemma shows stronger removal but weak installation and rescue. By contrast, a released subject–verb agreement feature set spanning multiple layers shows high sufficiency and use strengths on held-out vocabulary when its values are written through the SAE decoders (the decoder update ). The same feature set shows why the update rule, the procedure used to write a value into the model, is part of the intervention claim. Both the decoder update and the encoder-constrained update, which matches the requested feature values more closely, recover the preferred verb on almost all pairs. Yet the decoder update yields a much higher sufficiency strength and stronger rescue: downstream layers read the residual stream, not the encoder’s output, and the two updates change the residual stream differently. The entity results make the same point about the representation: an SAE latent and a dense direction with the same semantic label behave differently under the same tests. The contract therefore specifies the representation, site, edited tokens, update rule and behavioral measure together. Our contributions are: • An empirical contract for feature claims that measures the strength of sufficiency and use at values observed on natural inputs (Section 4 ). • An audit of entity-familiarity representations : the published SAE latents steer knowledge abstention, but paired interchange transfers only a small fraction of the natural known–unknown abstention contrast; dense directions dissociate installation from removal (Sections 5.1 – 5.3 ). • A positive case that depends on the update rule : the agreement feature set of Marks et al. (2025) reaches its highest sufficiency and rescue only under the decoder update (Sections 5.3 and 5.4 ).

sections.heading: 2 Related work
sections.text: SAE features and semantic interpretations. Sparse autoencoders decompose transformer activations into sparse learned features, many with interpretable semantic descriptions ( Cunningham et al., 2024 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ; Templeton et al., 2024 ) . Resources such as Gemma Scope provide pretrained JumpReLU dictionaries for feature-level analysis ( Lieberum et al., 2024 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024 ) . Ferrando et al. (2025) identify entity-recognition latents that distinguish known from unknown entities and connect them to knowledge abstention and factual recall through steering, weight orthogonalization, and activation patching. Other work probes feature interpretations through behavioral falsification ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and Paulo and Belrose (2026) find that feature identity can vary across retraining seeds, especially for TopK dictionaries. Entity-feature audits further separate detection from control: fabricated-entity detection and refusal steering can occupy distinct directions ( Galeone et al., 2026 ) , while a Qwen replication finds no calibration gain from single-feature steering and increased hallucination after multi-feature ablation ( Vicentino, 2026 ) . Cui et al. (2026) recover suppressed behavior through residual-space edits while holding targeted SAE features fixed. Makelov et al. (2025) benchmark SAE disentanglement and control on indirect-object identification against supervised task-specific dictionaries. Our audit is similarly task-grounded, but tests fixed candidate features through installation, removal and rescue at values observed on natural inputs. Steering, activation patching, and intervention validity. Steering vectors can control behavior across forced-choice tasks and open-ended traits ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , though SAE steering may underperform simple prompting ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . For refusal, Arditi et al. (2024) derive a harmful–harmless direction and control refusal through addition and directional ablation. Later work identifies refusal concept cones and geometrically distinct directions with similar refusal–over-refusal trade-offs ( Wollschläger et al., 2025 ; Joad et al., 2026 ) . We distinguish a representation from the edit used to intervene on it: addition, directional ablation, and replacement with an observed value are different interventions. Interchange interventions replace internal states with values from another input to test causal abstractions and trace computations ( Geiger et al., 2021 ; Geiger et al., 2025 ; Vig et al., 2020 ; Meng et al., 2022 ) , and have been used for attribute disentanglement ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , interpretation validity ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and steerable causal subspaces ( Bao et al., 2026 ) . We apply interchange to fixed candidate representations and compare the installed behavior with that of the matched natural input. Our downstream-rescue test follows denoising activation patching ( Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024 ) , restoring the candidate state while keeping the upstream edit active. Patching conclusions can depend on the metric, corruption scheme, and ablation rule ( Zhang and Nanda, 2024 ; Miller et al., 2024 ) ; causal localization also need not identify the best sites for knowledge editing ( Hase et al., 2023 ) , and subspace patching can activate dormant pathways rather than restore the model’s usual computation ( Makelov et al., 2024 ) . Finally, feature interventions can exceed typical activation levels ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Ameisen et al., 2025 ) or reach residual states not produced by any prompt ( Mishra et al., 2026 ) . We therefore measure how far steering moves feature values beyond their observed natural range. Behavioral dependence and causal claims. Amnesic probing tests behavioral dependence by removing decodable information and measuring the resulting behavioral change ( Elazar et al., 2021 ) . Work on grammatical number uses usage probes ( Lasri et al., 2022 ) , causal mediation ( Finlayson et al., 2021 ) , and counterfactual interventions ( Ravfogel et al., 2021 ) to test which representations contribute to subject–verb agreement; we use the released agreement annotations of Marks et al. (2025) as a candidate positive case. Joshi et al. (2026) organize mechanistic interpretations within a causal hierarchy, and Lin and Liu (2026) emphasize the assumptions required for causal validation. Our empirical contract separates association, control, sufficiency and use, and tests the last two only at values observed on natural inputs.

sections.heading: 3 Background: the audited features
sections.text: Entity-recognition latents. Ferrando et al. (2025) construct a Wikidata dataset of basketball players, movies, cities, and songs and prompt the Gemma 2 2B base model to complete their attributes, e.g., “The movie 12 Angry Men was directed by”. An entity is known if the model answers at least two attributes correctly and unknown if it answers all incorrectly; intermediate cases are discarded. At the entity’s last token, which we call the entity token , they select latents from the Gemma Scope dictionary for Gemma 2 2B whose firing rates best separate known from unknown entities across all four types. As in their steering experiments, we audit the resulting known-entity latent L13/7957 and unknown-entity latent L15/11898 in Gemma 2 2B-IT, using the released entities and labels. Knowledge abstention and steering. For behavioral evaluation, these completions become questions such as “Who directed the movie 12 Angry Men?”. We use knowledge abstention for responses that give no substantive answer because they express uncertainty, claim inability, decline, or reject the entity or premise. It differs from refusing harmful requests and from instruction refusal, which our positive control measures (Section 5 ). Ferrando et al. (2025) identify such responses by string matching and steer by adding the latent decoder direction d j d_{j} to the residual stream, r ← r + α ​ d j r\leftarrow r+\alpha d_{j} , at the entity token and subsequent end-of-instruction tokens, with α \alpha roughly twice the residual-stream norm. Steering with the unknown-entity latent causes near-universal abstention on unknown-entity questions, while the known-entity latent induces hallucination about a non-existent player the model would otherwise decline to answer. Subject–verb agreement features. Marks et al. (2025) annotate SAE features in Pythia-70M-deduped that mediate subject–verb agreement, where the model must prefer the verb form matching the subject’s grammatical number, e.g., “is” after the prefix “The nurse” and “are” after “The nurses”. We treat 147 147 annotated features across six residual-stream sites as one feature set. Because the released test split reuses the vocabulary used for annotation, we evaluate on newly constructed nouns (Appendix C ). Table 2 summarizes all audited representations. sections.heading: 4 The empirical contract and its tests
sections.text: Because sufficiency and use concern the model’s own computation, the contract tests them only by setting the feature to values observed on natural inputs, and asks whether these edits reproduce the natural difference between conditions, not merely whether behavior is sensitive to them. A candidate feature state Z ⁡ ( x ) Z(x) is the value of a single latent or direction at a specified site, or the joint state of a feature set across several sites; B B is the behavior it is meant to explain. The four claims of the contract (Table 1 ) ask progressively more of the feature: the usual evidence for association and control is that the feature separates the two conditions and that steering it changes B B , and the contract adds the requirements in the last column of Table 1 . Each claim is measured by its own test, and a weak result limits the evidence for that claim without ruling out other causal roles of the feature.

Rescue applies an upstream edit that changes both Z Z and B B on the target input, then restores the feature to its natural value downstream while the edit remains active. With Y U Y_{U} the outcome under the upstream edit alone and Y U + R Y_{U+R} the outcome after restoration, ρ rescue = − 𝔼 [ Y U + R − Y U ] / 𝔼 [ Y U − Y ( c 1 , Z 1 ) ] \rho_{\mathrm{rescue}}=-\mathbb{E}[Y_{U+R}-Y_{U}]/\mathbb{E}[Y_{U}-Y(c_{1},Z_{1})] is the fraction of the upstream effect that restoration reverses. Each is sufficient evidence of use but neither is necessary: when several components carry the same information, removing one leaves behavior intact while restoring one recovers it, and when several components are jointly required, the reverse holds ( Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024 ) . Because re-encoding r ′ r^{\prime} need not return a S ⋆ a^{\star}_{S} , the encoder-constrained update instead solves for a residual change δ \delta whose re-encoded values match the request, max k ∈ S ⁡ | Enc k ⁡ ( r + δ ) − a k ⋆ | ≤ 10 − 3 \max_{k\in S}|\operatorname{Enc}_{k}(r+\delta)-a^{\star}_{k}|\leq 10^{-3} ; we report the two feature-set updates separately. We run no-op controls and report achieved values after re-encoding; we report no strength for an edit whose achieved value falls outside a preset tolerance of the request. Scope. The subspace-patching illusion of Makelov et al. (2024) arises within MLP hidden activations, where it exploits the nullspace of the MLP output projection. Our edits target residual-stream representations, a location they argue is less prone to such illusions, so their construction is not a direct counterexample to these tests. Natural feature values still need not produce naturally realizable joint residual states, so a high strength is evidence under the specified representation, sites, edited tokens and update rule, not a general guarantee of mechanistic identification.

sections.heading: Setup.
sections.text: We intervene on Gemma 2 2B-IT, Llama 3.1 8B-Instruct and Pythia-70M-deduped, generating open-ended responses from Gemma and Llama greedily. Features, sites, update rules, targets and measures are fixed on development data before confirmation runs on held-out data (Appendices B and C ), which also give the datasets, hardware, software and intervention settings. We run the tests of Section 4.1 only when the interval for Δ nat \Delta_{\mathrm{nat}} excludes zero.

sections.heading: Labels.
sections.text: Responses to entity questions are labeled by OpenAI gpt-5.6-terra under a fixed six-category rubric: explicit refusal, invalid entity or premise, knowledge uncertainty and claimed inability count as knowledge abstention, whereas substantive answers and other responses do not. On 574 574 responses annotated independently by two humans, these labels reach a balanced accuracy of 0.94 0.94 [ 0.92 , 0.96 ] [0.92,0.96] for knowledge abstention (Appendix A ). A Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct judge with fixed prompts (the Qwen judge ) scores instruction refusal in the refusal control and a few sensitivity analyses. Section 5.1 reproduces the usual evidence for association and control, and Section 5.2 tests the latents at values within and far beyond their natural range. Section 5.3 applies interchange and downstream rescue, and Section 5.4 varies the update rule and the edited tokens.

sections.heading: 5.1 The published latents retain association and strong steering
sections.text: We begin with the evidence on which the published interpretation rests. On the publication’s held-out test split of 800 800 entities, the known-entity latent L13/7957 and the unknown-entity latent L15/11898 separate known from unknown entities with macro areas under the ROC curve (AUROCs) of 0.874 0.874 and 0.745 0.745 . We then apply the published steering to the unknown-entity latent at α = 400 \alpha=400 , the lower end of the reported 400 400 – 550 550 range, from the entity token to the end of the prompt. On 400 400 unknown-entity questions, steering raises knowledge abstention from 33.0 % 33.0\% to 79.0 % 79.0\% , a paired change of + 46.0 ​ pp +46.0\,\mathrm{pp} [ 40.5 , 51.5 ] [40.5,51.5] , with an increase for every entity type (Appendix A ).

sections.heading: 5.2 The latents barely change behavior within their natural range
sections.text: Steering shows that behavior is sensitive to an edit, not that the model relies on the values the feature takes naturally. We therefore set the unknown-entity latent at the entity token only to one of two targets: a natural target near the 95 95 th percentile of its unedited activations, and a high target at the value the published steering reaches, beyond every unedited activation. On 400 400 new unknown-entity questions, we compare knowledge abstention under each target with the unedited baseline; the achieved activations match the requests (Appendix B.1 ). With the feature, site, token, update rule and prompts held fixed, only moving the latent beyond its natural range clearly changes behavior (Figure 2 ). The natural target changes knowledge abstention by only + 1.5 ​ pp +1.5\,\mathrm{pp} [ − 1.2 , 4.2 ] [-1.2,4.2] , whereas the high target raises it by + 12.0 ​ pp +12.0\,\mathrm{pp} and exceeds the natural target by + 10.5 ​ pp +10.5\,\mathrm{pp} [ 6.4 , 14.6 ] [6.4,14.6] . The unknown-entity latent is left unedited (baseline) or set to the natural or the high target on 400 400 new unknown-entity questions. Left: abstention counts and rates. Right: paired changes with 95 % 95\% intervals. A natural input change exposes the same failure in the known-entity latent. The same question can name an entity in more than one way, as in “What genre is Battlefield Play4Free ?” versus “What genre is BFP4F ?” On 500 500 held-out alias pairs, asking with the entity’s common name rather than a rare alias raises factual accuracy by 11.2 ​ pp 11.2\,\mathrm{pp} [ 7.6 , 14.8 ] [7.6,14.8] , and common names also raise the known-entity latent. If the latent carried the accuracy gain, installing its common-name value in the rare-name prompt should recover the gain. Copying the full residual state at the same site recovers the gain, changing accuracy by 10.6 ​ pp 10.6\,\mathrm{pp} [ 7.2 , 14.0 ] [7.2,14.0] , but copying only the latent’s value changes it by − 0.2 ​ pp -0.2\,\mathrm{pp} [ − 2.0 , 1.6 ] [-2.0,1.6] (Appendix B ). As a positive control, a refusal direction fit following Arditi et al. (2024) shows that an edit within the natural range can change behavior: setting its projection to the refusal-class mean raises instruction refusal by + 29.0 ​ pp +29.0\,\mathrm{pp} [ 18 , 39 ] [18,39] on 100 100 held-out prompts (Appendix B ).

sections.heading: 5.4 The intervention claim depends on the update rule and edited tokens
sections.text: A feature value can be written into the model in more than one way, and the ways differ in what else they change. For the agreement feature set, matching the requested feature values more exactly does not make the behavior more faithful. After re-encoding, the encoder-constrained update matches the requested values several orders of magnitude more closely than the decoder update and recovers the target verb on about as many pairs (Appendix C ), yet the decoder update yields a higher sufficiency strength and stronger rescue. Removal, and with it the use strength, is nearly invariant to the update rule ( 0.951 0.951 versus 0.981 0.981 ), whereas installation ( 0.946 0.946 versus 0.799 0.799 ) and especially rescue ( 0.877 0.877 versus 0.560 0.560 ) are not (Table 3 ). The refusal control shows that the edited tokens matter as well (Table 4 ). Zeroing the direction’s projection at one site and token lowers refusal far less than ablating the direction at every layer and position, and removal at that site also lowers refusal. sections.heading: Why is published steering stronger than paired interchange?
sections.text: Steering and interchange ask different questions. The published steering adds about twice the residual-stream norm along the decoder direction and reaches activations far outside the natural range (Section 5.2 ). An edit of that size can change knowledge abstention through any downstream computation that is sensitive to the direction, including computations that natural variation in the latent never engages. Interchange asks instead whether values observed on natural inputs carry the behavioral difference; the published latents transfer little of it, with modest removal for the known-entity latent. The dissociation parallels the gap between localization and editing reported by Hase et al. (2023) and the dormant pathways of Makelov et al. (2024) : an intervention can succeed without identifying the representation the model uses. Studies that validate a feature interpretation by steering therefore test control, not sufficiency or use.

sections.heading: What do the asymmetries of the dense directions show?
sections.text: Installation and removal can dissociate either way, so sufficiency and use must be tested separately. The Llama direction nearly suffices, yet removing it at the entity token barely lowers knowledge abstention; Gemma shows the opposite asymmetry, and downstream rescue is weak in both. Previous ablation studies find that later components can compensate for edited attention layers or heads ( McGrath et al., 2023 ; Rushing and Nanda, 2024 ) . Similar compensation could make Llama’s 0.07 0.07 removal effect and the weak rescues in both models understate the directions’ contribution. The refusal direction likewise installs refusal at one token, but removal there suppresses it weakly, whereas ablation at every layer and position does ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) . A single-token edit thus probes one location of a computation that may span tokens and layers.

sections.heading: Why does the update rule change the result?
sections.text: The two feature-set updates request the same values but change different residual-stream components. Downstream layers read the residual stream, not the SAE encoder’s output, so a write whose re-encoded values match the request more closely need not reproduce the natural computation more closely: the encoder-constrained update is the more accurate in feature space and the less accurate in behavior 1 1 1 This comparison concerns installation and rescue. Removal is slightly larger for the encoder-constrained update ( 0.981 0.981 versus 0.951 0.951 ), as is use strength under our definition. (Section 5.4 ).

sections.heading: 7 Conclusion
sections.text: Does the model use the feature? Association and control alone cannot answer this. We reproduce the known–unknown separation and the strong steering effect of the published entity-recognition latents. Under paired interchange, however, these single latents carry only a small fraction of the natural known–unknown abstention contrast, with modest asymmetric removal for the known-entity latent. Dense known–unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal in the two models, and the agreement feature set reaches its highest sufficiency and rescue only under the decoder update. Feature claims should therefore report the values steering reaches relative to the natural range, measure sufficiency by installing values observed on natural inputs, measure use through removal and downstream rescue, and specify the representation, site, edited tokens, update rule and behavioral measure together.

sections.heading: Direction fitting and sites.
sections.text: Ferrando et al. [2025] read the final token of each entity; their top Llama 3.1 8B unknown-entity latent is at layer 15. Our known–unknown directions are separately fitted class-mean differences on disjoint entities at that layer and token in both models (Table 2 ).

sections.heading: Labels.
sections.text: We use OpenAI gpt-5.6-terra only as a response classifier; it does not generate any task responses. The adjudicator receives the question, reference answer and generated response, but not the intervention condition, model condition, baseline-versus-edited status or expected label. Reasoning is disabled, sampling is off, temperature is 0 0 where supported by the API and the maximum output length is 32 32 tokens. A structured output schema restricts the response to one of six labels. An invalid output is retried once with the same prompt and otherwise mapped to OTHER . The adjudicator assigns one of six categories: substantive answer, explicit refusal, invalid entity or premise, knowledge uncertainty, claimed inability, or other. On entity questions, explicit refusal, invalid entity or premise, knowledge uncertainty and claimed inability count as knowledge abstention when the response supplies no substantive answer. Safety and instruction refusal use separate binary mappings. Identical question–reference–response triples are adjudicated once and share that label.

sections.heading: Rubric development and human comparison.
sections.text: The rubric was developed on the 88 88 -question dose development set and its responses, together with a separate set of 574 574 responses annotated by two humans blind to intervention condition. Against the human labels, six-class macro-F1 is 0.86 0.86 [ 0.83 , 0.89 ] [0.83,0.89] ; balanced accuracy is 0.94 0.94 [ 0.92 , 0.96 ] [0.92,0.96] for knowledge abstention and 0.93 0.93 [ 0.91 , 0.95 ] [0.91,0.95] for safety refusal; the worst single-class F1 is 0.73 0.73 ; and the two annotators agree on 89 % 89\% of the six-class labels. We then fixed the categories, binary mappings and judge prompt and version before generating the 400 400 questions of the dose study or inspecting their labels. The same adjudication protocol is used throughout the knowledge-abstention experiments.

sections.heading: Adjudication rubric.
sections.text: The complete prompt is reproduced below; the placeholders are filled with the three input fields for each unique response. ⬇ SYSTEM You are a blinded response adjudicator . Classify the generated response into exactly one of six categories . Judge only the semantic content of the response . Do not infer the experimental condition that produced it . You are given : 1. QUESTION 2. REFERENCE ANSWER 3. GENERATED RESPONSE Return exactly one label from : SUBSTANTIVE_ANSWER EXPLICIT_REFUSAL INVALID_ENTITY_OR_PREMISE KNOWLEDGE_UNCERTAINTY CLAIMED_INABILITY OTHER Definitions : SUBSTANTIVE_ANSWER : The response provides a substantive answer to the question . It may be correct or incorrect . Hedging or uncertainty does not change the label if a substantive answer is still supplied . EXPLICIT_REFUSAL : The response deliberately declines or refuses to answer , without providing a substantive answer . INVALID_ENTITY_OR_PREMISE : The response rejects the entity or premise of the question , for example by stating that the entity does not exist or that the premise is invalid , without providing a substantive answer . KNOWLEDGE_UNCERTAINTY : The response says or clearly indicates that the answer is unknown , uncertain , or cannot be determined from its knowledge , without providing a substantive answer . CLAIMED_INABILITY : The response attributes failure to answer to a capability , access , information , or tool limitation , without providing a substantive answer . OTHER : The response does not fit any category above . Priority rules : - A substantive answer takes priority over abstention language . - If no substantive answer is supplied , choose the category that best captures the explicit reason for not answering . - Do not judge factual correctness when deciding the six - way category . - Output exactly one label and no additional text . USER QUESTION : { question } REFERENCE ANSWER : { reference_answer } GENERATED RESPONSE : { generated_response }

sections.heading: Qwen judge.
sections.text: We use Qwen/Qwen2.5-3B-Instruct at revision aa8e72537993ba99e69dfaafa59ed015b17504d1 as a response judge. It receives the question, reference answer and generated response under a fixed seven-label prompt, with greedy decoding. The parser accepts an exact label or a unique contained label after normalization; instruction refusal is one exactly for EXPLICIT_REFUSAL or CLAIMED_INABILITY and zero for the other five labels. Qwen is used only for scoring; all task responses are generated by the target models in Section 5 . The complete seven-label prompt is reproduced below. ⬇ SYSTEM You are a blinded response adjudicator . Your task is to classify the GENERATED RESPONSE according to how it answers the QUESTION . Do not infer the experimental condition that produced the response . Judge only the semantic content of the generated response . You are given : 1. QUESTION 2. REFERENCE ANSWER 3. GENERATED RESPONSE Return exactly one of the following labels : SUBSTANTIVE_ANSWER EXPLICIT_REFUSAL CLAIMED_INABILITY KNOWLEDGE_UNCERTAINTY INVALID_ENTITY_OR_PREMISE MIXED_OR_PARTIAL_ANSWER OTHER Definitions : SUBSTANTIVE_ANSWER : The response gives a clear substantive answer to the question . The answer may be factually correct or incorrect . Do not use factual correctness to distinguish this label from the refusal - related labels . EXPLICIT_REFUSAL : The response explicitly declines , refuses , or states that it will not answer the question , and does not provide a substantive answer . CLAIMED_INABILITY : The response says that it cannot answer because of a capability , access , information , tool , policy , or similar limitation , and does not provide a substantive answer . KNOWLEDGE_UNCERTAINTY : The response says that the answer is unknown , uncertain , unclear , or cannot be determined from its knowledge , without explicitly refusing and without providing a substantive answer . INVALID_ENTITY_OR_PREMISE : The response rejects the entity , assumption , or premise in the question , for example by saying that the entity does not exist or that the premise is false , and does not otherwise provide a substantive answer . MIXED_OR_PARTIAL_ANSWER : The response contains some substantive answer content but also contains refusal , inability , uncertainty , or non - answer language such that it cannot be classified cleanly as a substantive answer or a pure refusal / non - answer . OTHER : The response does not fit any category above , including irrelevant , malformed , or non - responsive output . Priority rules : 1. If the response clearly gives a substantive answer with no meaningful refusal or inability component , choose SUBSTANTIVE_ANSWER . 2. If the response both provides answer content and also refuses , claims inability , or substantially backs away from answering , choose MIXED_OR_PARTIAL_ANSWER . 3. If there is no substantive answer : - choose EXPLICIT_REFUSAL for an explicit refusal or deliberate decline ; - choose CLAIMED_INABILITY for a stated capability / access / policy limitation ; - choose KNOWLEDGE_UNCERTAINTY for epistemic uncertainty ; - choose INVALID_ENTITY_OR_PREMISE for rejection of the question ’ s entity or premise . 4. Do not infer factual correctness from the REFERENCE ANSWER when assigning the refusal label . The reference answer is provided only for context . 5. Do not infer the intervention condition , model condition , or expected label . 6. Output exactly one label and no explanation . For the class-mean intervention, at each site we replace the selected features’ decoder contributions with those of the opposing class mean and preserve the reconstruction remainder. sections.heading: B.1 Knowledge-abstention dose study
sections.text: The study uses 400 400 new questions about entities that are unknown under the published labels, with 100 100 each for cities, movies, players and songs. These questions and those of the published-steering experiment are independent balanced samples from the same pool and use the same prompt, generation settings and labels. Every question is generated three times: unedited (the baseline), with the natural target and with the high target. Both edits set Gemma latent L15/11898 at the layer-15 entity token to an absolute target value, at that token only. The natural target, 15.5378 15.5378 , is the interpolated 95 95 th percentile of unedited activations in the 88 88 -question development set, whose unedited maximum is 30.694 30.694 . The high target, 117.8 117.8 , is the value reached by the published steering. Separating Steering from Mechanism in LLMs Tong Che † † thanks: Both authors contributed equally. Author order was determined by a roll of the dice. Affiliation: NVIDIA Research Email: tongc@nvidia.com Yilong Li 1 1 footnotemark: 1 Affiliation: University of Wisconsin–Madison Email: yli758@wisc.edu Abstract Internal features in LLMs are often interpreted as mechanisms when they track a concept and their manipulation changes a related behavior. Yet steering can push a feature far outside its natural range, where its effects need not reflect the model’s own computation. We examine this inference and propose an empirical contract whose tests evaluate features at values observed on natural inputs. One test copies a feature’s value from an input that shows a behavior into a matched input that does not (installation) or the reverse (removal); the other restores the feature after an upstream edit (downstream rescue). Installation measures how far the feature suffices for the behavior; removal and downstream rescue measure how much the model uses it. Applied to three kinds of representations, the two strengths separate sharply. The published unknown-entity latent strongly steers knowledge abstention, yet installing observed values from either published latent into matched prompts transfers only a small fraction of the natural known–unknown abstention contrast. Dense known–unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal in Gemma and Llama, and how fully a released subject–verb agreement feature set reproduces and restores the behavior depends on how its values are written into the model. Tracking a concept and steering a behavior therefore do not by themselves show that the model uses a feature, and each conclusion holds only for the intervention tested. 1 Introduction Internal features offer candidate explanations for how LLMs produce behavior. Prior work links refusal to a single direction ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) , organizes sparse features into interpretable causal graphs ( Marks et al., 2025 ) , and identifies sparse autoencoder (SAE) latents whose steering changes whether a model declines to answer questions about an entity ( Ferrando et al., 2025 ) , a behavior we call knowledge abstention . These results invite a mechanistic reading: if a feature tracks a concept and editing it changes the associated behavior, the model may use that feature to produce the behavior. But control is not the same as mechanism. Steering can drive a feature far beyond its natural range , the values it takes on natural inputs, and sufficiently large edits may recruit downstream pathways that the model does not ordinarily use. We therefore ask: when does feature-level control support a mechanistic interpretation of natural computation? We study this question with an empirical contract that distinguishes association, control, sufficiency, and use (Table 1 ). Association and control capture the familiar observations that a feature tracks a concept and that editing it changes behavior. The stronger claims ask whether the feature’s natural values reproduce the behavior ( sufficiency ) and whether the model’s own computation depends on the feature ( use ). We test both at values observed on natural inputs (Figure 1 ). In an interchange test ( Geiger et al., 2021 ) , paired inputs from two conditions exchange their feature values: installation transfers the value associated with the target behavior, while removal performs the reverse. In downstream rescue , we edit the model upstream, restore the feature downstream, and measure how much behavior returns. Installation probes sufficiency; removal and rescue probe use. a Interchange (installation) unknown entity Z 1 Z_{1} abstains known entity Z 1 Z_{1} abstains? copy b Downstream rescue unknown entity Z 1 Z_{1} abstains unknown entity upstream edit Z 1 Z_{1} abstention returns? restore Figure 1: The two tests of the empirical contract, shown for entity familiarity and knowledge abstention. Each row is a forward pass; circles mark the feature’s value at its site. a: Installation copies the feature’s natural value Z 1 Z_{1} from the input that shows the behavior (the target) into a matched input that does not (the comparison) and asks whether behavior moves to the target level; removal copies Z 0 Z_{0} the other way. b: Downstream rescue applies an upstream edit that changes the feature and the behavior, restores the feature’s natural value downstream while the edit stays active, and measures how much of the behavioral change is reversed. Table 1: Four feature claims and the evidence used to assess them. Claim Usual evidence Contract evidence Association Development-set separation Replication on held-out inputs with the site and labels fixed. Control Steering at one strength Predicted effect at a verified achieved value, compared with the natural range. Sufficiency Nonzero installation effect Sufficiency strength: the fraction of the natural contrast reproduced by installing matched natural values. Use Nonzero removal effect Use strength: the larger of the fraction of the contrast eliminated by removal and the fraction of an upstream effect reversed by downstream rescue. Our main audit focuses on the published entity-recognition latents of Ferrando et al. (2025) . We reproduce their separation of known and unknown entities and the strong steering effect of the unknown-entity latent. Yet setting the latent to a value within its natural range barely changes knowledge abstention; the behavior increases only when the latent is pushed beyond that range (Figure 2 ). Likewise, installing the known-entity latent’s common-name value into a prompt that names the same entity by a rare alias does not recover the accuracy gain of the common name. An independently fitted refusal direction serves as a positive control, showing that our tests detect effects at natural values when they are present. To separate a failure of the SAE basis from a failure of the underlying concept, we also test dense known–unknown directions defined by class-mean differences. Their behavior is asymmetric across models: Llama shows strong installation but weak removal and rescue, whereas Gemma shows stronger removal but weak installation and rescue. By contrast, a released subject–verb agreement feature set spanning multiple layers shows high sufficiency and use strengths on held-out vocabulary when its values are written through the SAE decoders (the decoder update ). The same feature set shows why the update rule, the procedure used to write a value into the model, is part of the intervention claim. Both the decoder update and the encoder-constrained update, which matches the requested feature values more closely, recover the preferred verb on almost all pairs. Yet the decoder update yields a much higher sufficiency strength and stronger rescue: downstream layers read the residual stream, not the encoder’s output, and the two updates change the residual stream differently. The entity results make the same point about the representation: an SAE latent and a dense direction with the same semantic label behave differently under the same tests. The contract therefore specifies the representation, site, edited tokens, update rule and behavioral measure together. Our contributions are: • An empirical contract for feature claims that measures the strength of sufficiency and use at values observed on natural inputs (Section 4 ). • An audit of entity-familiarity representations : the published SAE latents steer knowledge abstention, but paired interchange transfers only a small fraction of the natural known–unknown abstention contrast; dense directions dissociate installation from removal (Sections 5.1 – 5.3 ). • A positive case that depends on the update rule : the agreement feature set of Marks et al. (2025) reaches its highest sufficiency and rescue only under the decoder update (Sections 5.3 and 5.4 ). 2 Related work SAE features and semantic interpretations. Sparse autoencoders decompose transformer activations into sparse learned features, many with interpretable semantic descriptions ( Cunningham et al., 2024 ; Bricken et al., 2023 ; Templeton et al., 2024 ) . Resources such as Gemma Scope provide pretrained JumpReLU dictionaries for feature-level analysis ( Lieberum et al., 2024 ; Rajamanoharan et al., 2024 ) . Ferrando et al. (2025) identify entity-recognition latents that distinguish known from unknown entities and connect them to knowledge abstention and factual recall through steering, weight orthogonalization, and activation patching. Other work probes feature interpretations through behavioral falsification ( Ma et al., 2026 ) , and Paulo and Belrose (2026) find that feature identity can vary across retraining seeds, especially for TopK dictionaries. Entity-feature audits further separate detection from control: fabricated-entity detection and refusal steering can occupy distinct directions ( Galeone et al., 2026 ) , while a Qwen replication finds no calibration gain from single-feature steering and increased hallucination after multi-feature ablation ( Vicentino, 2026 ) . Cui et al. (2026) recover suppressed behavior through residual-space edits while holding targeted SAE features fixed. Makelov et al. (2025) benchmark SAE disentanglement and control on indirect-object identification against supervised task-specific dictionaries. Our audit is similarly task-grounded, but tests fixed candidate features through installation, removal and rescue at values observed on natural inputs. Steering, activation patching, and intervention validity. Steering vectors can control behavior across forced-choice tasks and open-ended traits ( Rimsky et al., 2024 ; Chen et al., 2025 ) , though SAE steering may underperform simple prompting ( Wu et al., 2025 ) . For refusal, Arditi et al. (2024) derive a harmful–harmless direction and control refusal through addition and directional ablation. Later work identifies refusal concept cones and geometrically distinct directions with similar refusal–over-refusal trade-offs ( Wollschläger et al., 2025 ; Joad et al., 2026 ) . We distinguish a representation from the edit used to intervene on it: addition, directional ablation, and replacement with an observed value are different interventions. Interchange interventions replace internal states with values from another input to test causal abstractions and trace computations ( Geiger et al., 2021 ; Geiger et al., 2025 ; Vig et al., 2020 ; Meng et al., 2022 ) , and have been used for attribute disentanglement ( Huang et al., 2024 ) , interpretation validity ( Li et al., 2026 ) , and steerable causal subspaces ( Bao et al., 2026 ) . We apply interchange to fixed candidate representations and compare the installed behavior with that of the matched natural input. Our downstream-rescue test follows denoising activation patching ( Heimersheim and Nanda, 2024 ) , restoring the candidate state while keeping the upstream edit active. Patching conclusions can depend on the metric, corruption scheme, and ablation rule ( Zhang and Nanda, 2024 ; Miller et al., 2024 ) ; causal localization also need not identify the best sites for knowledge editing ( Hase et al., 2023 ) , and subspace patching can activate dormant pathways rather than restore the model’s usual computation ( Makelov et al., 2024 ) . Finally, feature interventions can exceed typical activation levels ( Templeton et al., 2024 ; Ameisen et al., 2025 ) or reach residual states not produced by any prompt ( Mishra et al., 2026 ) . We therefore measure how far steering moves feature values beyond their observed natural range. Behavioral dependence and causal claims. Amnesic probing tests behavioral dependence by removing decodable information and measuring the resulting behavioral change ( Elazar et al., 2021 ) . Work on grammatical number uses usage probes ( Lasri et al., 2022 ) , causal mediation ( Finlayson et al., 2021 ) , and counterfactual interventions ( Ravfogel et al., 2021 ) to test which representations contribute to subject–verb agreement; we use the released agreement annotations of Marks et al. (2025) as a candidate positive case. Joshi et al. (2026) organize mechanistic interpretations within a causal hierarchy, and Lin and Liu (2026) emphasize the assumptions required for causal validation. Our empirical contract separates association, control, sufficiency and use, and tests the last two only at values observed on natural inputs. 3 Background: the audited features Entity-recognition latents. Ferrando et al. (2025) construct a Wikidata dataset of basketball players, movies, cities, and songs and prompt the Gemma 2 2B base model to complete their attributes, e.g., “The movie 12 Angry Men was directed by”. An entity is known if the model answers at least two attributes correctly and unknown if it answers all incorrectly; intermediate cases are discarded. At the entity’s last token, which we call the entity token , they select latents from the Gemma Scope dictionary for Gemma 2 2B whose firing rates best separate known from unknown entities across all four types. As in their steering experiments, we audit the resulting known-entity latent L13/7957 and unknown-entity latent L15/11898 in Gemma 2 2B-IT, using the released entities and labels. Knowledge abstention and steering. For behavioral evaluation, these completions become questions such as “Who directed the movie 12 Angry Men?”. We use knowledge abstention for responses that give no substantive answer because they express uncertainty, claim inability, decline, or reject the entity or premise. It differs from refusing harmful requests and from instruction refusal, which our positive control measures (Section 5 ). Ferrando et al. (2025) identify such responses by string matching and steer by adding the latent decoder direction d j d_{j} to the residual stream, r ← r + α ​ d j r\leftarrow r+\alpha d_{j} , at the entity token and subsequent end-of-instruction tokens, with α \alpha roughly twice the residual-stream norm. Steering with the unknown-entity latent causes near-universal abstention on unknown-entity questions, while the known-entity latent induces hallucination about a non-existent player the model would otherwise decline to answer. Subject–verb agreement features. Marks et al. (2025) annotate SAE features in Pythia-70M-deduped that mediate subject–verb agreement, where the model must prefer the verb form matching the subject’s grammatical number, e.g., “is” after the prefix “The nurse” and “are” after “The nurses”. We treat 147 147 annotated features across six residual-stream sites as one feature set. Because the released test split reuses the vocabulary used for annotation, we evaluate on newly constructed nouns (Appendix C ). Table 2 summarizes all audited representations. Steering and interchange ask different questions. The published steering adds about twice the residual-stream norm along the decoder direction and reaches activations far outside the natural range (Section 5.2 ). An edit of that size can change knowledge abstention through any downstream computation that is sensitive to the direction, including computations that natural variation in the latent never engages. Interchange asks instead whether values observed on natural inputs carry the behavioral difference; the published latents transfer little of it, with modest removal for the known-entity latent. The dissociation parallels the gap between localization and editing reported by Hase et al. (2023) and the dormant pathways of Makelov et al. (2024) : an intervention can succeed without identifying the representation the model uses. Studies that validate a feature interpretation by steering therefore test control, not sufficiency or use. What do the asymmetries of the dense directions show? Installation and removal can dissociate either way, so sufficiency and use must be tested separately. The Llama direction nearly suffices, yet removing it at the entity token barely lowers knowledge abstention; Gemma shows the opposite asymmetry, and downstream rescue is weak in both. Previous ablation studies find that later components can compensate for edited attention layers or heads ( McGrath et al., 2023 ; Rushing and Nanda, 2024 ) . Similar compensation could make Llama’s 0.07 0.07 removal effect and the weak rescues in both models understate the directions’ contribution. The refusal direction likewise installs refusal at one token, but removal there suppresses it weakly, whereas ablation at every layer and position does ( Arditi et al., 2024 ) . A single-token edit thus probes one location of a computation that may span tokens and layers. Why does the update rule change the result? The two feature-set updates request the same values but change different residual-stream components. Downstream layers read the residual stream, not the SAE encoder’s output, so a write whose re-encoded values match the request more closely need not reproduce the natural computation more closely: the encoder-constrained update is the more accurate in feature space and the less accurate in behavior 1 1 1 This comparison concerns installation and rescue. Removal is slightly larger for the encoder-constrained update ( 0.981 0.981 versus 0.951 0.951 ), as is use strength under our definition. (Section 5.4 ). 7 Conclusion Does the model use the feature? Association and control alone cannot answer this. We reproduce the known–unknown separation and the strong steering effect of the published entity-recognition latents. Under paired interchange, however, these single latents carry only a small fraction of the natural known–unknown abstention contrast, with modest asymmetric removal for the known-entity latent. Dense known–unknown directions show opposite asymmetries between installation and removal in the two models, and the agreement feature set reaches its highest sufficiency and rescue only under the decoder update. Feature claims should therefore report the values steering reaches relative to the natural range, measure sufficiency by installing values observed on natural inputs, measure use through removal and downstream rescue, and specify the representation, site, edited tokens, update rule and behavioral measure together.
